newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhs' old capital plans underground railway.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhs' old capital plans underground railway.

text.p: A state construction firm in the Kazakh capital Almaty said on Wednesday the city planned to build a $600-$630 million underground railway system, even though the capital is moving this year to the northern town of Akmola.
"The metro will be a great relief for the city which is choked with traffic problems," Murat Ukshebayev, head of stated-owned city rail construction firm Almatymetrostroi, told Reuters in Almaty.
He said work on the project would start soon now that Canada's SNC-Lavalin Group Inc had presented the Kazakh authorities with a technical and financial description of the work.
Almatymetrostroi has already dug 7 km (4.3 miles) of tunnels and Ukshebayev said construction could start later this year or early 1998.
The planned length of the underground railway is 8.3-12.6 kilometres (5.0-7.8 miles), depending on which of three options presented by Lavalin is chosen by the authorities, Ukshebayev said.
The project will probably be financed by foreign banks, Ukshebayev said, although he said financing had yet to be studied fully by the government and Kazakhstan's state Eximbank.
The underground railway was started in the late 1980s when Kazakhstan was still a Soviet republic but work stopped as cash ran out following independence in 1991.
Ukshebayev appeared unconcerned that the Kazakh capital's move to the frozen steppe town of Akmola and Almaty's location in a seismic zone might hamper plans to build the railway.
He said 500,000 to one million passengers would use the underground daily, freeing Almaty's 1.5 million population from much of the air-polluting traffic.

On the earthquake-prone city, which is expecting a large quake sometime in the next decade, Ukshebayev said: "Japan is always shaken by earthquakes but their cities have their own metros. Why shouldn't we?"
